newsitem.title: CANADA: Placer tenure appears solid, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Placer tenure appears solid, analysts say.

text.p: Wary after high-profile ownership disputes over other big mineral discoveries, investors turned skittish Monday at news of a claim against Placer Dome Inc's Las Cristinas gold property, but analysts said Placer appeared to be on secure footing for now.
Crystallex International Corp said it acquired rights to two key blocks of Las Cristinas in Venezuela, where Placer aims to begin building a $576 million gold mine in May.
Placer vehemently disputed Crystallex's version of events, saying its tenure remains secure.
But Crystellex's announcement unnerved investors in light of recent disputes over big metal finds at Voisey's Bay in Canada and Busang in Indonesia.
Those disputes kept shareholders in the companies involved -- Diamond Fields Resources Inc and Bre-X Minerals Ltd -- in suspense for months amid fears that their tenure was in jeopardy.

Similar concerns took their toll on Placer stock Monday. The shares fell 1.60 to 27.75 in Toronto before recovering to 28.35. Crystallex stock meanwhile climbed 1.70 to 5.85 and then retreated to 4.70.

"None of these issues go away overnight," said Merrill Lynch analyst David Christensen. "If this got dragged out over time and into the courts, nobody would like to see that, especially if it delayed the project or raised investor concerns as to ownership."

The facts surrounding the Las Cristinas disputes were far from clear on Monday, spurring widespread confusion among analysts and investors. But based on the information available so far, analysts said Placer's rights appeared to be solid. "I don't think this will just die, but the onus is on Crystallex to prove its case," said Goepel Shields analyst Rick Cohen.

Crystallex said it obtained the rights by buying an unidentified Venezuelan company whose ownership of the concessions was confirmed by a Supreme Court decision last year. It did not say how much it paid for the rights.

But Placer said Venezuela has confirmed its tenure, granted under government contract in 1991. Moreover, it said last year's Supreme Court decision upheld the government's awarding of the property to Placer. The two blocks in dispute - four and six - contain most of Las Cristinas' nine million ounce reserves, analysts said. Placer has 70 percent of the property and a Venezuelan state-owned company the rest.

Christensen said the government's involvement in the project to date gives weight to Placer's argument. "It's an issue Placer believed was put to bed long before they started advanced drilling," he said.

A Placer spokesman said the company is making progress in raising US$250 million of financing needed for the project with a recent US$50 million commitment from a Latin American multilateral lending agency.

A US$80 million tax exoneration for project materials has been approved but not yet formally declared, he said. All the details including environmental permits are expected to be "nailed down by the end of May," he said.

While several analysts felt that Placer would ultimately prevail, they said Crystallex may try to negotiate a financial settlement. "At a certain point, it becomes cheaper just to pay someone to go away," said one analyst.

Crystellex said it was holding discussions with Placer but declined to say if it was negotiating to sell Placer its rights. Placer denied there were any talks and said it had no interest in negotiating with Crystellex.
